items.t: With U.S. Senate control at stake, Republicans fear the once-unthinkable: a blue Texas
items.x: (The Texas Tribune) - The last time a Democrat won statewide in Texas, James Talarico was in kindergarten. More than three decades later, in a state strewn with failed Democratic hopefuls once proffered as party saviors, the 37-year-old Austin Democrat is running neck-and-neck with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the most expensive U.S. Senate race in the country. Having failed to crack Talarico’s narrow yet stubborn polling edge, and with signs of tepid GOP turnout in early voting, Republicans are heading toward Election Day anxious about the once-unthinkable: Texas, the crown jewel of their national base, going blue. In the short run, control of the U.S. Senate could come down to the Lone Star State amid a tightly contested national map. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

Butler authorities say Kayla Dillenburg, 30, strangled a dog she pulled from an Indianapolis shelter, profited from donor pledges meant for its care, and admitted to the killing on a recorded phone call. Dillenburg, who operated Welcome Home Canine Rescue out of her residence, has been charged with torture or mutilation of a vertebrate animal, a felony, and fraud. Court documents stated Dillenburg pulled 21 dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care Services over a 10-day period in late April. Investigators allege she targeted animals carrying high financial pledges raised by social media donors trying to save shelter pets from euthanasia. items.t: Coroner identifies driver killed in Pickens County crash

The coroner identified the victim as 84-year-old Mylla Fisk Markland from Irmo. The coroner’s office said they were called to Highway 11 near Roy F. items.t: Kyle Chrisley pleads guilty to charges stemming from 2025 arrest, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Kyle Chrisley, son of reality television star Todd Chrisley, has pleaded guilty to resisting arrest in an incident from December 2025. Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. He was arrested Dec. 20 after his wife called police, reportedly saying he was “belligerent.” When police arrived, Chrisley reportedly punched multiple officers . items.x: COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS) - South Carolina SNAP recipients will no longer be able to buy some sugary items, including most candy and soda, starting Sunday, Nov. 1, under the program. The Healthy Food SC project - approved by the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food and Nutrition Service - will exclude candy, energy drinks, soft drinks, and sweetened beverages from the list of foods eligible for purchase under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as SNAP or food stamps. Diet and zero-sugar soft drinks will remain allowable purchases. How the program came about Gov. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Lincoln Mitchell, a political analyst and professor at Columbia University, says the first group feeling pressure is rural voters. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies. “We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. That’s really changed in the last year, where you see a much more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI,” Borick said. items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: Celebrating Halloween brings Wichita’s College Hill neighborhood together
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - While across the country, kids and families celebrate Halloween, one Wichita neighborhood has a celebration that feels a little more special. The rain and mud wasn’t enough to stop the crowds from trick-or-treating in College Hill, which has become a tradition for many Wichita families. “College Hill Halloween, we go big every year,” said Jeff Polson, who lives in the area. “We do something new every year.” This year, the Polson family decorated their home with a Dr. Suess theme in mind, complete with props, set pieces, costumes and music. “I grew up in College Hill, and when we moved back - I love Halloween. It’s the best holiday,” said Chloe Polson. “And so we needed to do something fun. And I love the idea of something different every year. And it’s a challenge for us to build it.” Related Story: Families in Wichita’s College Hill neighborhood describe hard work

items.t: ‘So well-received’: Last weekend of horse racing season at Eureka Downs
items.x: EUREKA, Kan. (KWCH) - Horse racing returned to Eureka Downs this season after a 16-year pause. Although it was a rainy weekend, the muddy track still brought thrills to fans, almost as if it never missed a beat despite its lengthy shutdown. A historic track in the sport, it’s the oldest surviving horse racing track west of the Mississippi River. Its first season dates back to 1903. Attendance waned in the 90s before it closed in 2011. Related Story: Eureka Downs prepares to host horse racing once again Last year, things changed when Governor Laura Kelly signed legislation into law that distributes tax revenues from historical horse racing wagering into funds intended to support live racing. The track is back, and so are the crowds. “We had two weekends with over 5,000 people showing up. items.t: Woman dies following head-on crash in Allen County
items.x: ALLEN COUNTY, Kan. (KWCH) - An Allen County woman is dead after an early morning head-on crash. The Kansas Highway Patrol said it happened just before 6:45 a.m. on Friday. A 15-year-old from Beloit was driving north on U.S. 169, seven miles south of Iola, when he crossed the center line and hit the woman’s vehicle head-on. First responders found the teenager in serious condition. He was taken to the hospital. The woman, identified as 66-year-old Sherry McDown from Iola, died at the scene.

items.t: 1-year-old boy dies after walking into road by home, troopers say
items.x: JONESVILLE, Fla. ( WCJB /Gray News) — A 1-year-old boy was hit and killed on a Florida roadway, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The crash happened in the Jonesville area Friday afternoon. Investigators said a car was headed west on Newberry Road when the boy entered the road from a nearby home. The driver didn’t see the child and hit him. The 1-year-old was taken to the hospital, where he died. Further information was not available.

The Buffaloes (3-5, 1-4 Big 12), who snapped a five-game losing streak, surrendered Blake Barnett’s 3-yard touchdown pass to Garrett Oakley with 2 seconds left in regulation, but kept the Wildcats (4-4, 1-4) to a field goal in the extra period. “It’s been a rough stretch, but we’re back on track now,” said Colorado linebacker Gideon ESPN Lampron, who had 15 stops, four tackles for loss and two of the Buffaloes’ five sacks. Facing third-and-9 from the 11, Wilson faked a handoff to Richard Young, who scored two touchdowns, and hit Williams over the middle for the game-winner. Showers and a few thunderstorms will become more numerous Sunday night over western and central Kansas as the main storm system approaches. The driver worked for Lynx EMS, a private ambulance company, and not for Cleveland EMS. According to Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975, once the driver left the patient, a Cleveland EMS unit responded to the scene. items.t: Salina man arrested for attempted second degree murder
items.x: SALINA, Kan. (KWCH) - One person was arrested in Salina for attempted murder on Friday. Salina police said that officers responded to Salina Regional Health Center on Friday after a 36-year-old man was brought to the ER with multiple stab wounds. Officers learned he had been stabbed while at his home in east Salina. Police identified and found the suspect, 28-year-old Daireese Gelinas, in a south Salina home. He was arrested without incident. The victim is in stable condition. Another man, who had attempted to separate the victim and the suspect, was also injured, but he was not hospitalized. Gelinas is charged with attempted second degree murder, aggravated assault and aggravated battery. The case is still under investigation.

items.t: Man posing as Amazon delivery driver accused of stealing multiple packages from neighborhood
items.x: LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. ( KPTV /Gray News) - A Portland man has been arrested after police say he stole packages while posing as an Amazon delivery driver. According to the Lake Oswego Police Department, 51-year-old Ramiro Despaigne Rodriguez was arrested on Oct. 21 after packages were reported stolen from at least eight homes in the Lake Oswego area. Police said the suspect was caught on surveillance video driving a car marked with a “delivery driver” sticker and wearing an Amazon vest. Rodriguez was arrested and booked into the Clackamas County Jail, where he faces first-degree theft charges. Investigators believe there may be more victims connected to this case.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

Dillenburg, who operated Welcome Home Canine Rescue out of her residence, has been charged with torture or mutilation of a vertebrate animal, a felony, and fraud. Court documents stated Dillenburg pulled 21 dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care Services over a 10-day period in late April. Investigators allege she targeted animals carrying high financial pledges raised by social media donors trying to save shelter pets from euthanasia. items.t: Kyle Chrisley pleads guilty to charges stemming from 2025 arrest, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Kyle Chrisley, son of reality television star Todd Chrisley, has pleaded guilty to resisting arrest in an incident from December 2025. Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. According to Us Magazine , the remaining charges were dismissed. He was arrested Dec. 20 after his wife called police, reportedly saying he was “belligerent.” When police arrived, Chrisley reportedly punched multiple officers . The lawsuit comes just days ahead of the midterm election, in which Marshall is running for re-election to the U.S. Senate. Meischa Zimmerman filed the lawsuit in the Barton County District Court, where Marshall’s practice once was. Zimmerman claims that Marshall charged her an illegal 18% interest on her $3,000 bill. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Stingray Cove ending 5-year run at Sedgwick County Zoo
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - Stingray Cove, a temporary interactive attraction at Sedgwick County Zoo, will conclude its run on Nov. 1, as its five-year contract with Living Exhibits concludes. The stingrays will be retained in Living Exhibits’ collection and moved to other locations. Stingray Cove opened in 2021 and has allowed guests to touch and feed cownose and Southern stingrays. The zoo said its success could lead to a permanent stingray habitat, included in a future phase of development under its master plan. items.t: Police respond to bomb threat at Wichita State University
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - Update 5:45 p.m.: Wichita State University has communicated that the bomb threat has been cleared and normal activities will resume. The investigation into the incident is ongoing. Police are responding to a bomb threat at Wichita State University. The university confirmed on Friday that WSU police received a threat of a bomb on the WSU campus, at the Hub for Advanced Manufacturing and Research, located at 1907 Innovation Blvd. The WSU campus community was alerted of the threat. Everyone inside the building was required to evacuate and were asked to stay away from the area until an all-clear is issued. University police are searching for any suspicious device, but none have been located as of 4:45 p.m. Since the threat is still being investigated, people are asked to avoid the area. This article will be updated as we learn more.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. (KWCH) - The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit ruled in favor of The Cozy Inn, a century-old burger restaurant, in a free speech fight with the City of Salina over a UFO-themed mural depicting flying burger-esque UFOs. In November of last year, a federal judge ruled in favor of the Cozy Inn, determining that the city violated the First Amendment by ordering the hamburger restaurant to stop the painting of the mural. items.x: BOSSIER PARISH, La. ( KSLA /Gray News) - A former high school band director facing dozens of sex offense charges is in critical condition after shooting himself during an arrest Thursday, authorities said. Williams was transported to an area hospital, where he remains in critical condition. Nicole Virzi, 32, pleaded guilty Wednesday to third-degree murder and other charges, avoiding a potential death penalty trial. She was sentenced to 35 to 80 years in prison. In 2024, Virzi was visiting Pittsburgh to assist her longtime friend, Savannah Roberts, with newborn twins Leon and Ari Katz, NBC News reported. When the parents took Ari to a hospital to treat unexplained injuries, Virzi offered to watch Leon. Later that night, Virzi called 911 claiming Leon fell from a baby bouncer. He was rushed to a children’s hospital, where he died. items.t: Dept. of Justice report shows efforts to combat elder fraud, abuse
items.x: TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW) - The U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Division released its annual report showing its efforts to combat elder fraud and abuse. The report summarizes the department’s enforcement, victim support, training, and other efforts to promote elder justice throughout the reporting period from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026. Over the year, the Department pursued nearly 350 criminal and civil enforcement actions involving fraud or abuse that targeted or affected older adults. The Department said about 96% of the cases were criminal in nature and 45% involved international schemes. These cases named 712 defendants who were charged with stealing or alleged to have stolen $4,841,305,931 from 711,353 victims. View the full report here: www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-releases-eighth-annual-elder-justice-report .

items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: NICU babies at Via Christi St. Joseph dressed up for Halloween
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - Halloween is sweet this year in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) at Via Christi St. Joseph in Wichita, where nurses and nurse techs helped the hospital’s tiniest patients celebrate their first Halloween in style. The care team hand-crafted costumes, including a bee, a butterfly, a flamingo, McDonald’s French fries, Winnie the Pooh and many more. The hospital said the special activity is a fun and meaningful way to share joy, creativity, and compassion with families spending the holiday in the NICU. Via Christi St. Joseph said the celebration reflects the dedication and heart the Via Christi care teams bring to every patient, every day.

items.t: Man posing as Amazon delivery driver accused of stealing multiple packages from neighborhood
items.x: LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. ( KPTV /Gray News) - A Portland man has been arrested after police say he stole packages while posing as an Amazon delivery driver. According to the Lake Oswego Police Department, 51-year-old Ramiro Despaigne Rodriguez was arrested on Oct. 21 after packages were reported stolen from at least eight homes in the Lake Oswego area. Police said the suspect was caught on surveillance video driving a car marked with a “delivery driver” sticker and wearing an Amazon vest. items.x: THOMASVILLE, Ga. (WALB) — A single mother of three is facing the fight of her life after doctors diagnosed her with Stage 4 non-small cell lung cancer that has spread to her brain. Kandis Hall, who worked three jobs to support her children before falling ill, said she was stunned when doctors delivered the news after she was hospitalized for a week. “At first I bust out crying. It was such a shock because I’ve never smoked a day in my life,” Hall said. “It’s still unbelievable. I still don’t believe it.” The cancer has metastasized to her brain, where doctors found five tumors causing severe memory loss, vision loss, and mobility issues. “I can’t hardly walk. I have a walker, but it doesn’t really help,” Hall said. “Everything was just a total shock to me. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

Butler authorities say Kayla Dillenburg, 30, strangled a dog she pulled from an Indianapolis shelter, profited from donor pledges meant for its care, and admitted to the killing on a recorded phone call. Dillenburg, who operated Welcome Home Canine Rescue out of her residence, has been charged with torture or mutilation of a vertebrate animal, a felony, and fraud. Court documents stated Dillenburg pulled 21 dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care Services over a 10-day period in late April. Investigators allege she targeted animals carrying high financial pledges raised by social media donors trying to save shelter pets from euthanasia. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

A lot of the instability is due to other processes that are very hard to forecast and represent in the numerical model,” Chipilski said. “The point of the project—sponsored by the National Science Foundation—is really to understand what makes a better forecast.” The need for improved nighttime forecasting is critical across the region. items.t: Man who walked into hospital with gunshot wound dies, Cleveland police say
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio (WOIO) - A man who walked into a hospital with a gunshot wound Saturday was later pronounced dead, Cleveland police said. Cleveland police say officers responded to 17200 Tarkington Avenue (Kerruish Park) for a report of shots fired at approximately 4:24 p.m. Police reported that, while responding, officers were told that a 22-year-old man had walked into a nearby hospital with a gunshot wound, where he was later pronounced dead. The Cleveland Police Crime Scene Unit responded to process the scene, and evidence was collected. The Homicide Unit is investigating.

It is also about standing behind a microphone, answering questions and refusing to let a stutter define his story. Concepcion, who has lived with a stutter for as long as he can remember, is now using his platform in the NFL to encourage others facing similar challenges. “My stutter has pretty much been here since I can remember talking for real,” Concepcion said. He went through speech therapy as a child, but building confidence was not always easy. His parents encouraged him to believe in himself and never let others take that confidence away. “My mom and dad just told me to always be confident. items.x: JONESVILLE, Fla. ( WCJB /Gray News) — A 1-year-old boy was hit and killed on a Florida roadway, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The driver didn’t see the child and hit him. The 1-year-old was taken to the hospital, where he died. Further information was not available.

items.t: Man posing as Amazon delivery driver accused of stealing multiple packages from neighborhood

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: Man dead, woman critically injured in Valley View crash involving motorcycle, Amazon semi
items.x: VALLEY VIEW, Ohio (WOIO) - One person is dead, and another was critically injured and transported for treatment following a crash that closed the intersection of Canal and Granger roads in Valley View Friday night. Valley View Police Chief Chris Bolton said the department’s dispatch center received a report at 9:07 p.m. of a crash involving an Amazon tractor-trailer and a motorcycle on Canal Road near the Amazon facility located at 5585 Canal Road. When officers arrived at the scene, they reported finding a man and woman on the motorcycle. Chief Bolton said the man was pronounced dead at the scene and the woman was critically injured and transported to MetroHealth Medical Center for treatment. Investigators from the police department were on scene investigating the crash along with members of the Southwest Accident Group (S.W.A.G.).

items.t: COVID-19 levels rising at Ashtabula wastewater treatment plant
items.x: ASHTABULA, Ohio (WOIO) - Health officials are urging residents to take simple precautions after an uptick in COVID-19 markers in untreated water. The city of Ashtabula Health Department says the Ohio Wastewater Monitoring Network has reported rising levels of the virus that causes COVID-19 in wastewater at the Ashtabula Wastewater Pollution Control Plant. The SARS-CoV-2 levels are described as increasing but currently moderate. Influenza levels remain low, and RSV was not detected in the most recent sampling. Officials say wastewater monitoring can act as an early warning system, with higher viral concentrations often appearing before increases in illnesses, reported cases and hospitalizations. The health department is asking residents to stay home when sick, practice good hand hygiene, and take extra care around people at higher risk for serious complications from respiratory infections

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.x: (Gray News) - Kyle Chrisley, son of reality television star Todd Chrisley, has pleaded guilty to resisting arrest in an incident from December 2025. Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. items.t: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

The driver didn’t see the child and hit him. The 1-year-old was taken to the hospital, where he died. Further information was not available.

items.t: Sanford Health surgeon weighs in on AI in surgery
items.x: BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR) - We’re already seeing artificial intelligence drive cars. But would you trust it to perform your next surgery? Most people still aren’t so sure. A nationwide Pew Research Center study found six out of ten Americans say they’d feel uncomfortable with doctors leaning on AI for their personal care. Still, about 40% think the technology could cut down on medical mistakes, even if letting machines take the scalpel sounds a bit far off. “We would need to see some big advancements in robotics,” surgeon Joshua Knudson said. “But I think if it can drive cars, it can probably learn how to operate as well.” For now, doctors say AI in the OR is strictly there to assist human hands, not replace them.

items.t: UND football drops second consecutive game on the road
items.x: BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR) - The University of North Dakota football team dropped its second consecutive game Saturday, falling 31-28 to No. 4 Youngstown State on the road. It was the No. 9 Fighting Hawks’ (6-4) final road game of the season and marks three consecutive road losses. 24 second half points were the difference maker as the Penguins flipped the script in the second half of the game. Quarterback Jerry Kaminski had a rushing, throwing and receiving touchdown in the game before the fourth quarter ever started. Kaminski also threw a pick six on the first drive in the second half. Up next, the Fighting Hawks host Illinois State next Saturday before a bye week on November 14.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: State audit reveals series of oversight issues with Health and Human Services
items.x: MINOT, N.D. (KMOT) - A new state audit found oversight problems across several North Dakota Health and Human Services programs. Auditors say more than 5,800 eligible children may have been missed by automated Summer EBT programs while some who were ineligible received benefits due to mismatched data. They estimated $217,000 in childcare benefits went to employees who did not meet hourly work requirements. The audit also revealed inadequate background checks for 45 in-home care providers.

items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Halloween 2026 statistics and forecast
items.x: BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR) - Halloween weather heavily shapes trick-or-treating plans, costume choices, and more. Here are some very spooky statistics for this weather-dependent holiday. Halloween falls in one of the most volatile months of the year. We’ve had years with cold and snow, but we’ve also had pretty nice Halloweens. In the last five years, we’ve seen it all. Last Halloween was a little chilly, with highs in the 30s and 40s. We had near normal temperatures in 2024 and 2021. The big jumps were back-to-back years of 2023 and 2022; from warm and well above normal temps in 2022 to cold, well below normal temps in 2023. You can see the differences even more per city. Take Bismarck for example: a record high of 7 degrees and a record low of 10 degrees below zero! Last year was pretty close to normal. Or Minot: the record temperatures are not as big of a swing, but more for a record snow.

Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. items.t: We The People: United Tribes Technical College Powwow
items.x: BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR) - Once a year, the United Tribes Technical College (UTTC) in Bismarck hosts Native Americans from across the country. This stop on the powwow circuit is known as the “Home of the Champions.” Dancers, singers and drummers can compete for cash prizes. Proceeds from the event go towards student scholarships at UTTC.

items.t: WAWSA seeks emergency assistance
items.x: WILLISTON, N.D. (KFYR) - The Western Area Water Supply Authority, which supplies clean water to thousands of people and businesses in five counties, is asking for emergency assistance from the state. The WAWSA board of directors said there are significant problems with the water intake at the treatment plant near Williston. While the water is still clear, sand and sediment at the intake has reduced capacity by 50%. And if it’s not fixed, it could have trouble meeting needs in Burke, Divide, McKenzie, Mountrail and Williams counties. “We need the State to step in to secure regulatory and funding assistance to replace or fix this crucially important infrastructure and prevent future water supply and treatment issues in the region,” Barke said. The board is asking Governor Armstrong to issue an emergency declaration to address the issue.

items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said. McDonald said the uneven turnout levels come from a partisan divide. “Registered Democrats, unaffiliated, those people who don’t have a party registration, are engaged at the moment. Earlier in the war, the president gave additional reasons for military action against Iran. items.t: Lawsuit challenges Virginia handgun purchase age, background check statutes
items.x: LYNCHBURG, Va. (WDBJ) - A new lawsuit in Lynchburg Circuit Court challenges two Virginia statutes on gun rights: one on whether adults 18 and older may buy handguns and one on universal background checks. Plaintiffs Melody Boyer and Natasha Rousseau are suing Virginia State Police Superintendent Jeffrey Katz. The attorney general’s office is representing Katz in the case. WDBJ7 contacted the office, which referred questions to Virginia State Police. WDBJ7 has not yet received a response from VSP. The plaintiffs say anyone 18 and older should be allowed to buy handguns. They also say universal background checks are unconstitutional. Gun Owners of America, GOA, has joined Boyer and Rousseau in the suit. items.t: Princeton Community Hospital hosts vendor bazaar for staff and visitors
items.x: BLUEFIELD, W.Va. (WVVA) - Princeton Community Hospital hosted a “Vendor Bazaar” for staff and visitors. The hospital’s volunteer program organized the event. Vendors included Fusion Permanent Jewelry, Monica’s Gifts for All and Blue Spoon Bakehouse and Catering of Bluefield. The event allowed people to begin holiday shopping and buy from small businesses in the two Virginias. “It’s so important to shop local during the holiday season and all year round. Supporting local is so, so important. That is the heart of your community,” said Nicole Coeburn, owner of Blue Spoon Bakehouse and Catering. Sellers displayed wreaths, lawn ornaments and other Christmas decorations.

items.t: McDowell County’s oldest living native celebrates 107th birthday
items.x: BLUEFIELD, W.Va. (WVVA) - Lydia Cathryn Payne Martin, the oldest living McDowell County native, celebrated her 107th birthday Friday with friends and family. Born in Bradshaw Martin was born Oct. 30, 1919, in the town of Bradshaw. She was one of 14 children. Proclamations presented Attendees presented Martin with two proclamations. One was from the state of West Virginia, and one was from the McDowell County commissioners. Family comments on longevity Martin’s family spoke about her health and longevity. Katie Litz, Martin’s niece, said, “She had a strong will, and I think, yes, she never seemed to let things bother her to the point that she couldn’t act like she wanted to.”

Kettering Foundation. Whitehead cited data from the Kettering Foundation and Gallup’s annual national survey of more than 23,000 adults. He said around 14% of the U.S. population strongly embraces Christian nationalism, with just over 16% at least sympathetic to it. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we address how aging and illness can impact intimacy, sharing practical ways for couples to talk openly and safely navigate sex after a diagnosis. Then, we discuss clinical trials, why older adults are frequently underrepresented and what questions to ask before participating in a study. Plus, we meet a 91-year-old world record holder in track and field proving that staying active has no age limit. When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear Health can affect intimacy as we age and the Aging Untold experts are addressing questions many couples are afraid to ask out loud: When is it safe to resume sex? items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: ‘Cultured Pearls’ craft quilts for Singing River cancer patients
items.x: PASCAGOULA, Miss. (WLOX) — On Friday the Theta Zeta Omega Chapter of the Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority delivered handmade quilts to the Singing River Cancer Center. A group called “The Cultured Pearls” is made up of all retired members of the sorority. They made the quilts with donated fabric, and wanted them to go to someone in need. The group has multiple cancer survivors who say they know firsthand how needed the quilts are. “I’m a breast cancer survivor, so I know when I was taking chemo, I was always getting cold,” Cathy Adams Mason said. “I know people and family members that have gone through especially for breast cancer and other cancers and to just do something for someone cause one day somebody may have to do that for us,” Edith McCovery said. In 1987, Boudreau owned an election supply and voting equipment company. She noticed a county in Washington state had started handing out stickers on Election Day. “It was black and white and had an X in a square. And that’s it. items.t: Man posing as Amazon delivery driver accused of stealing multiple packages from neighborhood
items.x: LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. ( KPTV /Gray News) - A Portland man has been arrested after police say he stole packages while posing as an Amazon delivery driver. According to the Lake Oswego Police Department, 51-year-old Ramiro Despaigne Rodriguez was arrested on Oct. 21 after packages were reported stolen from at least eight homes in the Lake Oswego area. Police said the suspect was caught on surveillance video driving a car marked with a “delivery driver” sticker and wearing an Amazon vest. Rodriguez was arrested and booked into the Clackamas County Jail, where he faces first-degree theft charges. Investigators believe there may be more victims connected to this case.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. MDOT recommends motorists take extra precautions during early morning and evening hours, when deer are more active. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: Man posing as Amazon delivery driver accused of stealing multiple packages from neighborhood
items.x: LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. ( KPTV /Gray News) - A Portland man has been arrested after police say he stole packages while posing as an Amazon delivery driver. According to the Lake Oswego Police Department, 51-year-old Ramiro Despaigne Rodriguez was arrested on Oct. 21 after packages were reported stolen from at least eight homes in the Lake Oswego area. Police said the suspect was caught on surveillance video driving a car marked with a “delivery driver” sticker and wearing an Amazon vest. Rodriguez was arrested and booked into the Clackamas County Jail, where he faces first-degree theft charges. Investigators believe there may be more victims connected to this case.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

Investigators allege she targeted animals carrying high financial pledges raised by social media donors trying to save shelter pets from euthanasia. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. Data from the South Carolina Election Commission shows that 110,172 votes were cast on Friday, bringing the statewide total to 948,592. Friday also marked the highest single-day turnout in the early voting period. The cumulative total is the highest early turnout for a gubernatorial election since the state began offering early voting in 2022. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Plane crashes near airports
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — For millions living in the shadow of an airport, the danger isn’t hypothetical. For one mother, it cost her everything. Plus, not every danger comes from above, sometimes it’s sitting right outside your window. That crash is now shining a light on millions of Americans who live or work in “Danger Zones” in close proximity to airports. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. According to Us Magazine , the remaining charges were dismissed. He was arrested Dec. 20 after his wife called police, reportedly saying he was “belligerent.” When police arrived, Chrisley reportedly punched multiple officers . He was arrested and released on an $88,500 bond. People reported that he was arraigned in July before his plea hearing in September.

Caden Bradley took the toss, found the edge and ran about 70 yards for a touchdown. The extra point was no good, and Tioga led 6-0 in the first quarter. Shane Platukis then scored a touchdown for Tioga. Tioga continued to score, and the Tigers won 44-14.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Lincoln Mitchell, a political analyst and professor at Columbia University, says the first group feeling pressure is rural voters. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies. “We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. items.t: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said. items.x: McDONOUGH, N.Y. (WBNG) — American Legion Post 1478 is calling on neighbors to roll up their sleeves as it hosts its first-ever community blood drive on Monday, Nov. 2. The drive runs from noon to 5 p.m. at McDonough Town Hall, 1178 County Road 5. The Sons of the American legion commander for Post 1478 said this is the legion’s inaugural drive and is urging community members to come out and help make it a success. Donors with Type O, A-negative or B-negative blood are encouraged to consider a Power Red donation to double the impact. To schedule an appointment, donors can call 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767) or visit RedCrossBlood.org and enter the code McDonough. According to the Red Cross, individuals who donate blood will receive a $10 Amazon gift card via email and 200 bonus points toward donor rewards. More details can be found at rcblood.org/Maze .

items.t: Endicott Fire Department responds to dumpster fire in Endicott
items.x: ENDICOTT, N.Y. (WBNG) — The Endicott Fire Department (EFD) responded to a report of a dumpster fire across the street from Visions Federal Credit Union on McKinley Avenue on Thursday, Oct. 29, according to a Facebook post . Upon arrival, crew found a large red roll-off dumpster filled with burning construction debris. Flames reached approximately 15 feet high. According to the EFD, an improperly discarded cigarette caused the fire. Firefighters acted immediately, as flames threatened a nearby building. They quickly contained the fire before it spread. The EFD is urging people to completely put out cigarettes before throwing them away. “A cigarette takes seconds to discard. The damage it can cause can last a lifetime,” EFD said.

items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said.
