items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

Ranger describes securing the man “When I got out to him and was trying just to get him secured to me, the thought went through my mind, ‘If we both slip before I have him clipped in and on my tether, he’s dead. items.t: Woman sues NE Portland motel, saying it ignored signs of child sex trafficking
items.x: PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - A woman is suing the Aaron Motel in northeast Portland, alleging that she was a victim of sex trafficking beginning at the age of 13 and that the motel ignored the signs. The lawsuit alleges that for decades, commercial sex traffickers have openly operated in and out of hotels on 82nd Avenue, including the Aaron Motel. The woman says she was trafficked through the Aaron Motel between 2021 and 2024. She says that due to familiarity with employees at the motel, they would allow her to rent a room as a child, often accompanied by older men, and returning the motel key as soon as 30 to 60 minutes later. She is seeking $5 million in damages from the motel. FOX 12 is working to contact the owners of the Aaron Motel for comment and will update this story if they respond.

Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. According to Us Magazine , the remaining charges were dismissed. He was arrested Dec. 20 after his wife called police, reportedly saying he was “belligerent.” When police arrived, Chrisley reportedly punched multiple officers . He was arrested and released on an $88,500 bond. People reported that he was arraigned in July before his plea hearing in September.

items.t: Man accused of stealing packages in Lake Oswego while dressed as Amazon driver
items.x: LAKE OSWEGO Ore. (KPTV) - A Portland man was arrested after allegedly stealing packages in Lake Oswego while posing as an Amazon delivery driver, police said on Friday. According to the Lake Oswego Police Department, 51-year-old Ramiro Despaigne Rodriguez was arrested on Oct. 21 after packages were reported stolen at eight homes across the city. Police said the suspect was caught on surveillance video driving a car marked with a “delivery driver” sticker and wore an Amazon vest. Rodriguez was arrested and booked into the Clackamas County Jail, where he faces first-degree theft charges. Investigators believe there may be more victims connected to this case (Case #26-5469), and asked anyone with information to contact Lake Oswego police at (503) 635-0238.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: Daimler closes truck manufacturing plant in north Portland; Lays off 375 workers
items.x: PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - A truck manufacturing plant in northwest Portland closed for good on Friday, laying off almost 400 workers. Daimler Truck North America made the announcement in July, saying 375 positions would be eliminated. In July, the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers union issued a statement in response: “Our employer’s decision to leave the Portland area does not remove the heart and soul that our members have put into their work at Daimler. And the IAM will support and fight for our members regardless of any decision their employer makes.” Officials at Daimler say while their Portland factory is closing, the city will continue to serve as their North American headquarters. Production will be moved to Daimler’s facilities in the Carolinas.

items.t: Oregon Zoo treating Tula-Tu for virus that killed another baby elephant
items.x: PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - Veterinary teams at the Oregon Zoo have started intensive treatment for an Asian elephant calf, Tula-Tu, infected with elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus, or EEHV. Staff noticed changes in the behavior and energy levels of the calf, Tula-Tu, on Oct. 24. Technicians found a low white blood cell count during routine in-house screening, prompting veterinarians to start antiviral medications immediately, the zoo said in a statement shared with FOX 12 on Friday. The Oregon Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at Oregon State University confirmed an elevated viral load of EEHV the following day, leading the care team to administer plasma transfusions. Another baby elephant housed at the Oregon Zoo, 6-year-old Lily, succumbed to the virus in 2018. But staff say there’s hope this time. “Early detection is critical,” said Dr. Carlos Sanchez, the zoo’s animal health director.

items.t: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said. McDonald said the uneven turnout levels come from a partisan divide. “Registered Democrats, unaffiliated, those people who don’t have a party registration, are engaged at the moment. items.x: PORTLAND, Ore. (KPTV) - Guard Ja Morant will be out for at least four weeks after suffering a hamstring injury, the Portland Trail Blazers announced Friday. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. items.t: Ambulance driver accused of abandoning patient, said he was ‘done driving for the day’ and called an Uber home
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio ( WOIO /Gray News) — An ambulance driver is accused of abandoning a patient he was transporting to the hospital earlier this week in Ohio. The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Texas man killed in single-vehicle crash on I-10 near Creole/Cameron exit
items.x: LAKE CHARLES, La. (KPLC) - A Texas driver died Thursday afternoon following a single-vehicle crash along I-10 East near the Creole/Cameron exit. The crash happened shortly before 4 p.m., according to Louisiana State Police Troop D. A preliminary investigation shows a 2025 Ford Escape was heading east when it veered off the right side of the roadway and struck a tree. The driver, a 43-year-old Montgomery, Texas, man who was not wearing a seat belt, died at the scene. The crash remains under investigation.

items.t: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Lincoln Mitchell, a political analyst and professor at Columbia University, says the first group feeling pressure is rural voters. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies. “We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. That’s really changed in the last year, where you see a much more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI,” Borick said. items.t: Trump to make final midterm stops in Iowa and Kansas Sunday
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will make final campaign stops in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, two days before Tuesday’s midterm elections. Trump won Iowa three times and Kansas twice. He is hoping to give Republicans a final boost in both states. He originally scrapped the stops but decided at the last minute to go through with them. The Senate seats in both states are a must-win for Republicans to hold the chamber. A recent Marist poll shows Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson trailing Democrat Josh Turek by three points in Iowa. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton holds a narrow lead over incumbent Republican Roger Marshall for the first time. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he is not worried. “I’ve seen the voters on the ground. I’m telling you, the polls are wrong. They’re inaccurate. items.t: At the oldest building in New Orleans, voices from the past come to life in new exhibit
items.x: NEW ORLEANS (WVUE) - Completed around 1752, the Old Ursuline Convent in the French Quarter is said to be the oldest surviving building in the Mississippi River valley. Now the Old Ursuline Convent Museum, there’s a new exhibit marking 300 years since the Ursuline nuns arrived in New Orleans. Sarah Waits, senior archivist at the Archdiocese of New Orleans, said back then, the sisters landed in a developing colony. “It was a wilderness. They talk about the mosquitoes and the alligators and just a huge cypress forest, and there were buffalo grazing along the river. It was a wild place,” said Sarah Waits. According to archdiocesan archives, 12 Ursuline nuns came to New Orleans in 1727 and eventually left the French Quarter in 1824. items.t: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said. McDonald said the uneven turnout levels come from a partisan divide. “Registered Democrats, unaffiliated, those people who don’t have a party registration, are engaged at the moment. items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The number of Americans who identify with Christian nationalism is slightly declining, but religion remains a large part of politics for both candidates and voters ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. “We see where Americans fall on this spectrum of Christian nationalism, which really tells us a lot about what they think democracy is and how it’s functioning,” said Andrew Whitehead , a professor of sociology at Indiana University Indianapolis and a research fellow for the Charles F. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.x: JONESVILLE, Fla. ( WCJB /Gray News) — A 1-year-old boy was hit and killed on a Florida roadway, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. items.t: Smell of smoke prompts Delta flight to make emergency landing in Atlanta
items.x: ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — A Delta flight made an emergency landing in Atlanta on Saturday due to a “smoky odor,” the airline said. Delta Flight 1264 from Chicago to Atlanta declared an emergency before it touched down at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport just before 8 a.m. The plane was greeted by fire trucks on the tarmac before it taxied to the gate on its own. The plane, a Boeing 737-900, carried six crew members and 130 passengers. No injuries were reported. Delta did not say what caused the smoky smell. This is a developing story. Check back with Atlanta News First as we learn more.

Boudreau said she has long supported voting, which she described as the right and duty of American citizens to share their voice. “This is the one day that we have to amplify what we want our world to look like, and it just irritated me and my folks, too, when people would say, oh I forgot the election,” Boudreau said. In 1987, Boudreau owned an election supply and voting equipment company. She noticed a county in Washington state had started handing out stickers on Election Day. “It was black and white and had an X in a square. And that’s it. items.t: Shooting leads officers to find drugs, cash at Austell home, police say
items.x: ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — A shooting investigation led Austell police officers to find suspected drugs and tens of thousands of dollars in cash, according to the department. Police were called to a residence at around 1 a.m. on Saturday, where they found a man with a gunshot wound to the abdomen. His wife was taken into custody as the suspect. During a search of the home, officers said they found more than 300 grams of suspected cocaine, suspected marijuana and more than $34,000 in cash. items.t: Man posing as Amazon delivery driver accused of stealing multiple packages from neighborhood
items.x: LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. ( KPTV /Gray News) - A Portland man has been arrested after police say he stole packages while posing as an Amazon delivery driver. According to the Lake Oswego Police Department, 51-year-old Ramiro Despaigne Rodriguez was arrested on Oct. 21 after packages were reported stolen from at least eight homes in the Lake Oswego area. Police said the suspect was caught on surveillance video driving a car marked with a “delivery driver” sticker and wearing an Amazon vest. Rodriguez was arrested and booked into the Clackamas County Jail, where he faces first-degree theft charges. Investigators believe there may be more victims connected to this case.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

Butler authorities say Kayla Dillenburg, 30, strangled a dog she pulled from an Indianapolis shelter, profited from donor pledges meant for its care, and admitted to the killing on a recorded phone call. Dillenburg, who operated Welcome Home Canine Rescue out of her residence, has been charged with torture or mutilation of a vertebrate animal, a felony, and fraud. Court documents stated Dillenburg pulled 21 dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care Services over a 10-day period in late April. Investigators allege she targeted animals carrying high financial pledges raised by social media donors trying to save shelter pets from euthanasia. items.t: UGA researchers study impact of rising temperatures on gator eggs
items.x: ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — The Florida Gators might be the Bulldogs’ rivals on the field, but off the field, researchers in Athens are trying to save real-life gators. A team of researchers studied 146 alligator eggs, incubating them under five temperature ranges between 86 and 93 degrees Fahrenheit. Alligators are a species with temperature-dependent sex determination, meaning the temperature at which an egg incubates determines the sex of the embryo. More extreme temperatures tend to result in females, while moderate temperatures result in males. Critically, the temperatures in these ranges fluctuated when most studies incubate at a constant temperature. The team found that, at higher temperatures, the results differed substantially from those of eggs incubated at constant temperatures. items.t: Man stabbed by brother in Marietta, leading to hours-long standoff, police say
items.x: ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — A man was stabbed by his brother in Marietta on Friday, leading to an hours-long standoff with officers, according to police. Officers with the Marietta Police Department responded to a dispute between family members that involved physical violence at a home on North Saint Marys Lane just before 9:30 a.m., a department spokesperson said. A 40-year-old man had been stabbed in the shoulder, and said he had been stabbed by his younger brother. He was treated for non-life-threatening injuries. Jeffrey White, 38, remained uncooperative for hours before negotiators persuaded him to come outside and surrender, police said. He has been charged with aggravated assault and aggravated assault with a weapon. This is a developing story. Check back with Atlanta News First for updates.

items.t: Man killed in Cobb County car crash identified, police say
items.x: ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — A man killed in a Cobb County car crash Wednesday has been identified, according to police. Police said Marc A. Beltran, 25, was driving east on Akers Mill Road around 2 a.m. Wednesday when he tried to make a right turn onto Cumberland Boulevard, but instead went through the intersection and crashed into a concrete barrier. An ambulance took him to Wellstar Kennestone Hospital, where he died. Police said speed is believed to be a contributing factor. The crash remains under investigation. Anyone with information should contact Cobb County police at 770-499-3987.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. items.t: Buford woman convicted of scamming seniors out of $1 million, Gwinnett County DA says
items.x: ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — A Buford woman has been convicted of scamming seniors out of around $1 million, the Gwinnett County district attorney said. Starting in 2021, Fataoumata Keita, 48, scammed seniors as part of a larger operation. She convinced her victims their computers were malfunctioning and that they needed to buy antivirus software. They would then be directed to a 1-800 number, where conspirators posing as customer service representatives told the victims to mail checks to a post office box in Buford. Keita would then pick up the money and distribute it to her co-conspirators. The scam racked up as much as $1 million. Keita was convicted of violating Georgia’s Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act. She will be sentenced in December.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Mom to Mom: From heartbreak to hope, Forrest Spence Fund helps thousands of Tennessee families
items.x: MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - October is Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month. For one Memphis mother, losing her newborn son changed her life forever. From that heartbreak came a mission to help other families in their darkest days. From that heartbreak came the Forrest Spence Fund — a nonprofit created in honor of her son to help other families in their darkest days. Nineteen years ago, Brittany and David Spence were living through a parent’s worst nightmare. Their newborn son, Robert Forrest Spence, was rushed to Le Bonheur Children’s Hospital, where he spent 55 days fighting for his life. “I held Forrest as he died in my arms, and my husband held me as he died in the only place he’d ever known, which was Le Bonheur Pediatric ICU,” said Brittany Spence, co-founder of the Forrest Spence Fund. items.t: AirBnB ramps up Halloween anti-party technology in Memphis as neighbors call for peace and quiet
items.x: MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Airbnb is activating heightened anti-party technology across Memphis this Halloween weekend, aiming to stop disruptive house parties before they start. The short-term rental company has enforced a global ban on disruptive parties since 2020. However, during high-volume holiday weekends like Halloween and the Fourth of July, the company deploys automated booking defenses targeting higher-risk reservations. “We look at hundreds of different signals to determine if a reservation might be of a higher risk of a party,” said Javier Hernandez, Senior Communications Manager at Airbnb. “This can include things like whether or not the reservation was made last minute or the proximity of the person who made that reservation to the address of that listing.” During Halloween weekend last year, Airbnb says the algorithm deterred roughly 195 people in Memphis from booking entire

items.x: MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - A man is fighting to survive, and Memphis Police are investigating after a shooting in the Bethel Grove neighborhood Friday. A gunshot victim was dropped off at Fire Station #22 on Lamar Avenue following a shooting just after 5 p.m. The man was transported to the hospital in critical condition. A crime scene was later discovered at Semmes Street and Wildrose Street. Police said that a black Nissan SUV fled the scene. This is now an active investigation. items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Tillman police station transforms into a haunted house for the community

Memphis police have an alternative for you and your little ghouls and goblins on Friday night. Officers have turned the Tillman Station into a haunted house! Like, we just get to come out, and they get to have a good time, we get to have a good time, and I think it’s good for everybody to get together in something that’s not enforcement capacity,” Major Adam Pickering said. items.t: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Lincoln Mitchell, a political analyst and professor at Columbia University, says the first group feeling pressure is rural voters. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies. “We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. That’s really changed in the last year, where you see a much more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI,” Borick said. items.t: Ark. inmate captured after assaulting officers during escape
items.x: BRINKLEY, Ark. (WMC) - Arkansas State Police located a man accused of assaulting officers and escaping custody. Investigators said 41-year-old Rodney Smith escaped on foot from the Brinkley Detention Center on Thursday morning. Smith was being held at the facility while awaiting bed space with the Arkansas Division of Correction. Smith allegedly assaulted law enforcement personnel and stole and officer’s Taser during his escape. Smith was spotted as a passenger in a vehicle on Lee County Road 310 on Friday. Smith and the driver, Marshall Jones, were taken into custody and taken to the Arkansas Division of Correction East Arkansas Regional Unit in Brickeys. Smith is a convicted felon whose criminal history includes aggravated robbery and domestic battery. Click here to sign up for our newsletter! Click here to report a spelling or grammar error. items.t: Trump to make final midterm stops in Iowa and Kansas Sunday
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will make final campaign stops in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, two days before Tuesday’s midterm elections. Trump won Iowa three times and Kansas twice. He is hoping to give Republicans a final boost in both states. He originally scrapped the stops but decided at the last minute to go through with them. The Senate seats in both states are a must-win for Republicans to hold the chamber. A recent Marist poll shows Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson trailing Democrat Josh Turek by three points in Iowa. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton holds a narrow lead over incumbent Republican Roger Marshall for the first time. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he is not worried. “I’ve seen the voters on the ground. I’m telling you, the polls are wrong. They’re inaccurate. items.t: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said. McDonald said the uneven turnout levels come from a partisan divide. “Registered Democrats, unaffiliated, those people who don’t have a party registration, are engaged at the moment. items.t: Trump says Iran war goal met as gas prices rise
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S.-led war against Iran, which began February 28, has affected every part of America. Now it may play a critical role in the upcoming midterm elections. President Donald Trump launched the war with one major objective: preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Earlier in the war, the president gave additional reasons for military action against Iran. At a recent campaign rally, Trump said that goal has already been met. “We obliterated Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer, Operation Epic Fury,” Trump said. “We defeated them militarily, financially and otherwise. And now we are ensuring just one thing: we have to make sure that they never, ever have a nuclear weapon, and we will do that very easily.” Trump has made that declaration numerous times. items.t: The relationship between Christian nationalism and Americans’ views of democracy
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The number of Americans who identify with Christian nationalism is slightly declining, but religion remains a large part of politics for both candidates and voters ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. “We see where Americans fall on this spectrum of Christian nationalism, which really tells us a lot about what they think democracy is and how it’s functioning,” said Andrew Whitehead , a professor of sociology at Indiana University Indianapolis and a research fellow for the Charles F. Kettering Foundation. Whitehead cited data from the Kettering Foundation and Gallup’s annual national survey of more than 23,000 adults. He said around 14% of the U.S. population strongly embraces Christian nationalism, with just over 16% at least sympathetic to it. items.t: Gov. Bill Lee appoints interim commissioner of Tennessee Department of Corrections
items.x: What This Story Is About Gov. Bill Lee has appointed Christopher Hansen as interim commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction. Why It Matters Hansen steps in to lead the state’s prison and supervision system following the October resignation of former Commissioner Frank Strada after the botched Sept. 30 execution of Christa Pike. What Happens Next Hansen assumes the interim commissioner role effective immediately while continuing to oversee TDOC’s probation and parole operations during the leadership transition. For Context Before joining TDOC in 2023, Hansen spent decades in public safety and corrections leadership, including chief probation officer roles in California and Nevada, as well as positions in Florida. Nicole Virzi, 32, pleaded guilty Wednesday to third-degree murder and other charges, avoiding a potential death penalty trial. She was sentenced to 35 to 80 years in prison. items.t: Aging Untold: When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we address how aging and illness can impact intimacy, sharing practical ways for couples to talk openly and safely navigate sex after a diagnosis. Then, we discuss clinical trials, why older adults are frequently underrepresented and what questions to ask before participating in a study. Plus, we meet a 91-year-old world record holder in track and field proving that staying active has no age limit. When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear Health can affect intimacy as we age and the Aging Untold experts are addressing questions many couples are afraid to ask out loud: When is it safe to resume sex? items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: 2 people, 5 dogs rescued from Olive Branch house fire
items.x: OLIVE BRANCH, Miss. (WMC) - Two people and five dogs were rescued Thursday night after a house fire broke out along Oak Leaf Drive. The Olive Branch Fire Department responded to the home around 7 p.m. When crews arrived, they helped an elderly woman and two dogs safely evacuate. The woman was transported to a local hospital for evaluation. Firefighters then entered the home, encountering heavy smoke and flames spreading through the kitchen and living room. During a search, crews located a elderly man trapped inside a back bathroom. He was rushed to Regional One Health and treated for smoke inhalation and esophageal burns; officials expect him to make a full recovery. Firefighters also found three more dogs inside the house, rescuing and treating them on scene. Investigators determined the fire started in the kitchen, though the exact cause remains under investigation. Click here to sign

items.t: 1-year-old boy dies after walking into road by home, troopers say
items.x: JONESVILLE, Fla. ( WCJB /Gray News) — A 1-year-old boy was hit and killed on a Florida roadway, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The crash happened in the Jonesville area Friday afternoon. Investigators said a car was headed west on Newberry Road when the boy entered the road from a nearby home. Winter is the six-year-old girl with autism who died tragically on a hot day on a daycare bus on August 13. items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The “I Voted” sticker given to people who cast ballots began with one woman, Janet Boudreau, who designed it after seeing a local county hand out a different sticker on Election Day. Boudreau said she has long supported voting, which she described as the right and duty of American citizens to share their voice. “This is the one day that we have to amplify what we want our world to look like, and it just irritated me and my folks, too, when people would say, oh I forgot the election,” Boudreau said. In 1987, Boudreau owned an election supply and voting equipment company. She noticed a county in Washington state had started handing out stickers on Election Day. “It was black and white and had an X in a square. And that’s it. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: U.S. Steel breaks ground on $1.9 billion building
items.x: OSCEOLA, Ark. (KAIT) - U.S. Steel broke ground Friday on a $1.9 billion direct reduced iron facility at its Big River Steel Works campus in Osceola. The project connects U.S. Steel’s Minnesota iron ore mines directly to its electric arc furnaces in Mississippi County. The massive capital investment is expected to create 200 full-time jobs. “Community is always important to a project like this,” Jim Bell said, vice president of operations and construction engineering, “Big River employs 1,800 employees right now; to add another 200 in this rural part of Arkansas always means a lot to these counties.” Brown projects the buildout to take 32 months, including a year of engineering and equipment delivery followed by two years of on-site construction. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Jackson fire chief warns residents as fires continue under burn ban
items.x: JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT) — Most of the state, including Hinds County, is under a burn ban, but a string of fires has broken out across the city of Jackson. The Jackson Fire Department said the city has seen an influx of fires in the past few weeks and is asking residents to help prevent them. Some of the fires are being investigated as arson, and officials said others started because of simple carelessness. Officials said that under the current burn ban, even a small spark can lead to a felony charge. Jackson Fire Chief RaSean O. Thomas said people are responsible for the fires they cause. “If you throw a cigarette butt out of the window, and you cause a fire, you can burn someone’s home, you can burn someone’s property,” Thomas said. “… That is part of your responsibility to make sure you dispose of it properly. But if you do not and you cause a fire, you’re responsible for that as well.”

Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: 2 people, 5 dogs rescued from Olive Branch house fire
items.x: OLIVE BRANCH, Miss. (WMC) - Two people and five dogs were rescued Thursday night after a house fire broke out along Oak Leaf Drive. The Olive Branch Fire Department responded to the home around 7 p.m. When crews arrived, they helped an elderly woman and two dogs safely evacuate. The woman was transported to a local hospital for evaluation. Firefighters then entered the home, encountering heavy smoke and flames spreading through the kitchen and living room. During a search, crews located a elderly man trapped inside a back bathroom. He was rushed to Regional One Health and treated for smoke inhalation and esophageal burns; officials expect him to make a full recovery. Firefighters also found three more dogs inside the house, rescuing and treating them on scene. items.t: ‘I Voted’ sticker creator talks about how it started

Boudreau said she has long supported voting, which she described as the right and duty of American citizens to share their voice. “This is the one day that we have to amplify what we want our world to look like, and it just irritated me and my folks, too, when people would say, oh I forgot the election,” Boudreau said. In 1987, Boudreau owned an election supply and voting equipment company. She noticed a county in Washington state had started handing out stickers on Election Day. “It was black and white and had an X in a square. And that’s it. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: City of Brundidge to kick off annual Peanut Butter Festival
items.x: BRUNDIDGE, Ala. ( WSFA ) - To most, peanut butter is just a staple spread in the pantry. But in Brundidge, it represents heritage, resilience, and decades of community pride. Crowds are already gathering along South Main Street in downtown Brundidge as the town prepares for the 35th Annual Brundidge Peanut Butter Festival, an event that draws thousands to Pike County each year. The roots of the festival trace back to the Great Depression, when the peanut industry provided crucial economic relief to local families during difficult times. “Just seeing the continuous stream of people all day long coming here for the same thing... something that was an ordinary food back in the day that united this community, that helped during a time where just about everyone around was destitute,” said Austin Green, guidance counselor at Pike Liberal Arts School. “It happened during the Great Depression.”

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities.
